content: A wafer in electronics refers to a thin slice of semiconductor material, such as a silicon crystal, which is utilized in the manufacturing of integrated circuits and other microdevices. The wafer acts as the substrate upon which microelectronic devices are constructed, both within and on the surface of the wafer. During its production, the wafer undergoes numerous microfabrication processes, including doping or ion implantation, etching, deposition of various materials, and photolithographic patterning. Wafers are created from highly pure, nearly defect-free, single-crystalline materials. One common method for producing crystalline wafers is the Czochralski growth process, which was developed by the Polish chemist Jan Czochralski. In this process, a cylindrical ingot of high-purity crystalline silicon is formed by pulling a seed crystal from a molten silicon bath. The resulting ingot is then sliced using a diamond-coated blade and polished to create wafers. These wafers are typically produced in sizes up to 12 inches (300 mm) in diameter. Semiconductor fabrication plants, also known as fabs, are categorized based on the size of wafers they are equipped to produce. Over time, wafer sizes have increased to enhance production efficiency and reduce costs. The current state-of-the-art fabs are designed to handle 300 mm (12-inch) wafers. The thickness of wafers varies depending on their diameter, with typical thicknesses ranging from 275 µm for smaller wafers to 775 µm for 12-inch wafers. Wafers made from materials other than silicon are generally not available in sizes larger than 100 mm and may have different thicknesses compared to silicon wafers of the same diameter. The thickness of a wafer is determined by the mechanical strength of the material, ensuring it can support its own weight without cracking during handling. For any given wafer diameter and target integrated circuit (IC) size, the exact number of individual die pieces that can be cut from the wafer can be calculated. This is referred to as the gross die count, which can be estimated using a specific mathematical formula. However, this calculation does not account for losses due to defects, alignment markings, or test sites on the wafer. When wafers are sliced, their surfaces are aligned according to specific crystallographic orientations, defined by the Miller index. These orientations are critical because the structural and electronic properties of a single crystal are highly anisotropic. For example, the depth of ion implantation can depend on the wafer's crystal orientation. Additionally, wafer cleavage typically occurs along well-defined directions, allowing the wafer to be easily scored and diced into individual chips (or dies), which contain billions of circuit elements. Wafers smaller than 200 mm in diameter often have flat edges cut into one or more sides to indicate crystallographic planes of high symmetry, such as the {110} face, and to denote the wafer's orientation and doping type. In modern wafers, a notch is used instead of flats to convey this information, minimizing material waste. Silicon wafers are not composed of 100% pure silicon but are instead doped with impurities such as boron, phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony. These impurities are introduced during the melting process at concentrations ranging from 10¹³ to 10¹⁶ atoms per cm³, defining the wafer as either n-type or p-type. The wafers may also contain interstitial oxygen, while contamination from carbon and metallic impurities is minimized. For electronic applications, transition metals must be kept at concentrations below parts per billion to ensure optimal performance. While silicon is the most commonly used material for wafers in the electronics industry, other compound semiconductors, such as III-V or II-VI materials, are also employed. Gallium arsenide (GaAs) wafers, for instance, are a widely used III-V semiconductor material and can also be produced using the Czochralski process.
